subtopic: CANADA AND ITALY, ROUMANIA, HUNGARY AND FINLAND TO BE SIGNED AT PARIS THIS DAY

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretaiy of State for External Affairs): Today in Paris treaties of peace will be signed between Canada and four of her former enemies. From July to October of last year, Canada was represented at a conference in Paris which was called to consider draft peace treaties with Italy, Roumania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Finland. These treaties have now been completed, and in the ceremony of signature in Paris, Canada will be represented by the Canadian Ambassador to France, Major General Vanier. The treaties are subject to ratification and will come into force with respect to Canada when they have been approved by parliament and when an instrument of ratification has been deposited. The treaty with Bulgaria will not be signed by Canada; we were not at war with that country.
The Canadian delegation to the Paris conference was led by the right honourable the Prime Minister. The other members of the delegation w:ere the Minister of National Defence, who at that time was minister of national health and welfare; the Canadian Ambassador to France and the Canadian Ambassador to the U.S.S.R.; the head of the Canadian military mission to Germany; Mr. N. A. Robertson, at that time Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, and Mr. Arnold Heeney, clerk of the Privy Council. These representatives were accompanied by several advisers from the Department of External Affairs. When the Prime Minister returned to Canada during the latter part of August, my colleague the Minister of National Defence assumed the leadership of the delegation.
The conference at Paris wras restricted, through the terms of reference given it by the council of foreign ministers, to the function of examining draft peace treaties which had been prepared by the council and to making recommendations on these draft treaties for the further consideration of the four foreign ministers. No assurance was given to the seventeen states which joined the four great powers at Paris that the recommendations of the conference would be accepted by the council of foreign ministers which was to prepare the final texts of the treaties. On the contrary, the United Kingdom, the United States of America, the Soviet Union and France came to the Paris
Peace Treaties

conference committed to support those articles of the draft peace treaties on which previous agreement had been reached. It was only in respect of the unagreed articles, therefore, that the states attending the Paris conference were allowed any real freedom of action.
In these circumstances the opportunity given us to influence the settlements under discussion at Paris was not great. The Prime Minister in his opening address made known to the conference Canada's misgiving over procedures which permitted so limited a participation in the work of peace-making. Canada, he said, had a vital interest in these treaties and desired to see them established on principles of justice and equity which would lead to a lasting peace.
In spite of the limitations imposed on the conference at Paris, it was nonetheless possible for the Canadian delegation to make a valuable contribution to the drafting of the peace treaties, particularly in respect of articles which had not previously been agreed upon by the council of foreign ministers. The Paris conference was able to adopt, by the necessary two-thirds majority, a number of recommendations which were subsequently used in the New York meetings of the council of foreign ministers as a basis for discussion. The principles of these recommendations were in many cases adopted and incorporated in the final texts. Such important questions as the establishment of the free territory of Trieste, the freedom of the Danube, the settlement of disputes arising out of the interpretation or execution of the treaties, and the settlement of the amounts of reparation payable by the ex-enemies to the allies, were all of this category. The conference also did useful work in clarifying and improving the text of many articles in both agreed and unagreed sections of the treaties. In this connection, the present Minister of National Defence, in his capacity as chairman of the legal and drafting commission, made a particularly useful contribution to the conference.
I should like now to table the final texts of the treaties with Italy, Roumania, Hungary and Finland as signed today in Paris. I wish also to table a statement prepared by the Minister of National Defence, which will supplement the few remarks I have made on this subject. For the convenience of the house, I would ask that this statement, which covers some eight pages of single-space typewriting and which would be rather lengthy to put on

Hansard, be printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings. It would then be available to all hon. members.
The final texts of the treaties will be published in the Treaty Series by the Department of External Affairs, and copies will be made available to all members in due course and before the matter is brought before the houses of parliament for ratification.

Provided that nothing in this subsection shall operate to prevent a minister of the crown from communicating to the Senate or to the House of Commons any information obtained under the provisions of this act.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MEETINGS-ATTITUDE OF CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVES ON THE FRANCO GOVERNMENT
INTERNATIONAL MEETINGS-ATTITUDE OF CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVES ON THE FRANCO GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
1.	Since the end of hostilities, what were the international meetings in which Canadian representatives took part and in the course of which the question of the Franco government was brought up?
2.	What questions concerning the Franco government were brought to the attention of the representatives of the nations?
3.	What was the attitude of the representatives of Canada on each of such questions?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	The question of the Franco government was brought up at the San Francisco conference, at the first part of the first session of the general assembly of the United Nations, at the second part of the first session, at the sessions of the economic and social council, at meetings of a number of its commissions and committees, and at meetings of specialized agencies.
2.	At these meetings proposals were made ranging from a break in diplomatic and economic relations with Spain to condemnations of the Franco government.
3.	The general attitude of the Canadian government was set forth in the statement made by the representative of Canada on December 3, 1946, to the political and security committee of the general assembly. This statement includes the following passages;
We abhor the record and the present policies of Franco dictatorship.
We earnestly hope that the Spanish people may be able to rid themselves of Franco by peaceful means and establish a democratic responsible and enlightened administration.
We are not prepared to support at this time outside intervention in Spain which might impede European recovery, or revive in Spain the horrors and sufferings of civil war.
A new civil war in Spain is not likely to result in the establishment of a moderate and democratic regime. We do not wish to be instrumental in substituting one form of despotic or totalitarian rule for another. We want the Spanish people to enjoy the blessings of freedom-freedom from dictatorships whatever their form, by whatever name they may be called . . .
We feel that the question of the participation of any state which is not a member of the United Nations in any specialized agency should be decided on one basis only-the practical advantages to the peoples of the United Nations of the government of that state being committed to the obligations of membership in that agency. This is the position which the. Canadian government has consistently maintained in the meetings of the economic and social council and of the specialized agencies. In our opinion no useful purpose is served by limiting the scope or weakening the effectiveness of the specialized agencies in order to debar the Franco government from the obligations of membership in them.
Questions

The complete text of the statement will be included in the report of the Canadian delegation to the second part of the first session of the general assembly which will be tabled in the near future. This report will also contain a record of the votes cast by Canada on the eight main proposals placed before the general assembly and the text of the resolution adopted by the general assembly on December 12, 1946. The Journal of the United Nations (No. 50 of December 5, 1946, pp. 245-6) contains a summary of the Canadian statement of December 3, 1946. The text of the general assembly's resolution of December 12, 1946, is given in the Journal (No. 75: supplement A-64, add. 1, pp. 825-6).

subtopic: INSPECTION OF IMPORTED BULBS
INSPECTION OF IMPORTED BULBS
speechtext:
1.	Is there any official bulb standard for (a) bulbs grown in Canada; (b) imported bulbs?
2.	Is there any inspection of bulbs entering Canada ?
3.	What steps are taken to prevent diseased bulbs and bulbs infected with mites entering Canada?

subtopic: INSPECTION OF IMPORTED BULBS
speechtext:
1.	(a) No official bulb standards nor any regulations pertaining to the production of bulbs in Canada have been established. However, in the case of British Columbia particularly, plant pathologists attached to the Dominion Plant Pathological Laboratory at Saanichton, B.C., have devoted a good deal of time during the past few years in assisting bulb growers of that province in the propagation of bulbs, the detection of bulb diseases and pests, and methods of control.
1. (b), 2 and 3. Bulbs imported into Canada are subject to the provisions of Regulation No. 1 (Foreign) Destructive Insect and Pest Act. It is required that a permit to import be obtained in advance from the plant protection division; that all shipments must be accompanied by a certificate of inspection issued in the country of origin covering freedom from injurious insects and plant diseases; that all consignments be routed through one of the established ports of importation, and all importations are subject to reinspection by the plant protection division before final release to the consignee. This requirement, as applying to bulbs, has been in effect since 1928.
In carrying out reinspections in Canada, no specific standards apply with respect to size as importations are dealt with on the basis of freedom from injurious insects and serious plant diseases. In the case of common diseases, tolerances are allowed which vary according to the kinds of bulbs and the diseases involved. In some cases, importations may be released with a minor tolerance; in others, resorting to eliminate the hazard may be authorized and in still others, particular lots of bulbs in the consignment may be refused entry.

May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether payments of the 1943 participation certificates have yet been concluded, and if so when we may expect commencement of payment of the 1944 certificates?
The Canadian wheat board has disposed of the 1944-45 wheat crop. However, at the present time the Canadian wheat board is engaged in making up and sending out cheques covering the 1943 crop payment. The board is also involved in the adjustment payment of 10 cents per bushel, raising the initial payment covering the 1945 crop deliveries from $1.25 per bushel basis One northern, to $1.35 per bushel. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: * CABINET COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall give an oral answer to this question. The question relates to the proceedings and organization of the cabinet. Because of the general principle of collective responsibility of the cabinet it has always been recognized that matters of the kind referred) to are necessarily secret.
In this connection I would refer hon. members to Campion's "An Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons, 1929" at pages 129-130, in which it is stated that among questions deemed1 out of order as infringing constitutional propriety are those- -seeking information about matters which are in their nature secret, such as decisions or proceedings of the cabinet (including the committee of imperial defence and other committees of the cabinet).
If further authority is required I might refer the house to an extract from an address on the machinery of government made by the Right Hon. Sir John Anderson in May of last year, from which I quote the following brief extract:

It has been the general practice of governments to refuse to disclose in public the functions or the composition of cabinet committees. This practice, which will no doubt be maintained, rests upon the theory that decisions are those of the government as a whole, and that the internal arrangements which may be made by ministers for discussion among themselves are essentially a domestic matter and no concern of parliament or the public.
This quotation is taken from the "Machinery of Government" by the Right Hon. Sir John Anderson, the "Romanes Lecture", May 14, 1946, pages 17-18.
In replying to a similar inquiry by a member of the United Kingdom House of Commons in November, 1945, as to the names of the chairman and members and as to the functions of the manpower committee of the United Kingdom cabinet, the Right Hon. Herbert Morrison replied as follows:
Mr. Garry Allighan asked the prime minister whether he will state the names of the chairman and members of the manpower committee.
Mr. H. Morrison:	No, sir. The arrangements made by the cabinet for the discharge of the business for which it is collectively responsible are matters for the cabinet itself and are not customarily disclosed.
Mr. Garry Allighan:	Will the lord president
of the council say whether this committee is entirely advisory, or can take decisions in regard to matters?
Mr. Morrison:	To answer that would be a
breach of the doctrine to which I have just referred.
The quotations I have just read may be found in the United Kingdom House of Commons Debates of November 12, 1945, column 1744.
While this aspect of the collective character of the cabinet's responsibility to the House of Commons is quite clear, it is open to the government in its discretion to give such information and make such explanations as may be deemed advisable from time to time. For example, during the war I had occasion to inform the house of special wartime committees of the cabinet which had been set up to deal with the peculiar problems of the war period and to assist ministers in discharging the especially heavy and complicated duties which then fell to their lot.
At present there do exist a number of committees of the cabinet, for the preliminary examination of different questions of policy coming before the government for decision. Some of these are standing committees, such as that which has to do with defence and that dealing with reconstruction problems. Others are of a temporary ad hoc character. The responsibility of the cabinet, however, remains a collective responsibility and organization into committees is merely a matter of procedural convenience. The membership of

Questions
such committees is designated from time to time by the Prime Minister, or the cabinet, according to the subject matter under consideration.
As to the hon. member's inquiries concerning secretaries or clerks provided to cabinet committees, this is a duty normally performed by members of the staff of the privy council office, or occasionally by officials assigned for the purpose from other appropriate departments of government. The remuneration of such officials is determined in the usual way in relation to the duties which they perform in the privy council office or in such other department. The functions of such committee secretaries are secretarial only and in no sense executive. They prepare agenda under the direction of committee chairmen, make such records of committees' proceedings as may be deemed appropriate, and perform such other related tasks as the committees may direct.

subtopic: * CABINET COMMITTEES
speechtext: May I ask a question with respect to the answer given by the Prime Minister? He has drawn upon a certain precedent with respect to procedure to justify denial of the answers to the questions asked. My question is this. Does the Prime Minister wish that decision to apply to every question asked in that list? Some of us thought that we should not be denied the details of the construction of the executive council and committee connected therewith, but there are several other questions. Does not the Prime Minister wish to deny information in connection with, say, 6 and 7-who acts as secretary or clerk of each committee, and what salary is he paid?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: * CABINET COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I have stated the position with regard to the collective responsibility of the cabinet and with respect to the proceedings in the cabinet. That is a fundamental principle of cabinet government. There may be questions that hon. members may wish to ask in regard to particular matters. They will be considered in the light of the general statement I have just made. It may be they can be answered without any question arising. If, however, they invalidate the principle that has been laid down, the answer will have to be that the information is not to be disclosed.
My hon. friend asks who acts as secretary or clerk of each committee. I should not think that was information that should be given to the public. The committees of the cabinet are confidential committees. They are there for the purpose of assisting the government in reaching a decision. Many of them are advisory. Who is chosen for one committee or another is a matter for cabinet decision and should be so regarded. My hon. friends asks, what salaries are paid. All questions of salary will be public in the statement which appears with respect to salaries of officials. The house is of course free to ask for information in regard to any salary of any official. That will be given as such and not as part of a disclosure of proceedings of the cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: * CABINET COMMITTEES
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has asked that question. He knows that the clerk of the council also acts as secretary of the cabinet. Where the clerk of the council is also secretary of the cabinet, he does receive a larger salary than he would receive as clerk of the council. Has the government been consulted or advised by either the government of Great Britain or any of the dominions on the abandonment of the Suez canal and Cairo military base by Great Britain?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	Commonwealth governments keep each other informed on matters of foreign policy in accordance with the practice described by Mr. Attlee, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, in the House of Commons in London, on May 8, 1946, as follows.
It is our practice and our duty as members of the British commonwealth, to keep other members of the commonwealth fully and continuously informed of all matters which we are called upon to decide, but which may affect commonwealth interests. The object is to give them an opportunity of expressing their views in confidence, if they so desire. These views are taken fully into account, but the decision must be ours, and the other governments are not asked, and would not wish, to share the responsibility for it. Dominion governments follow the same practice.
This practice has been followed with respect to United Kingdom policy in Egypt.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, might I be allowed to answer a question that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day. The question, was:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Will he lav on the table, as soon as possible, the report of the Canadian delegation to the preparatory world trade conference? At the same time, will he

25S
World Trade Conference

indicate what instructions were given to the Canadian delegation and what attitude was taken by that delegation? Who will be the Canadian representatives to the next trade conference, and what instructions will they be given by the government?
The answer is as follows:
The Canadian delegation did not prepare a separate report because of the arrangements made by the united nations for publishing the proceedings of the first session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment. This report has now been issued by the united nations, and I table a copy. Copies are. available in the parliamentary library and the Department of External Affairs is endeavouring to obtain additional copies from the united nations for the use of members. Copies in the French language have not yet arrived but are expected shortly from London.
The proceedings of the first session held in London in October and November 1946, were exploratory and did not involve any commitments on the part of the governments concerned. The character of the deliberations is made evident in the following excerpt from the report:
Before attempting to outline the work accomplished at the first session, it is desirable to emphasize that this is a "preparatory" committee, the task of which is to prepare an annotated agenda for an international conference and that it is only at the final stage, that is, at the conference, that governments will enter upon binding commitments. However, it is clear that a thorough discussion by the officials of a large number of the world's principal trading nations in advance of the conference will greatly facilitate the work of the conference itself. This conception of the task of the preparatory committee is essential for a full understanding of the nature and significance of the report which follows.
The Canadian delegation accordingly was not given detailed instructions but was given the general responsibility of exploring on the official level ways and means of overcoming barriers to world trade and of otherwise expanding the volume of world trade on a multilateral basis.
The second session scheduled for Geneva in April will be a continuation of the work of the preparatory committee. The Canadian delegation will act under the same general terms of reference, with a view to preparing for the united nations conference. Included in the work of the second session will be negotiations looking toward reciprocal and mutually advantageous tariff concessions.
The Canadian delegation will be headed by Mr. Dana Wilgress, Canadian. Ambassador to the U.S.S.R., with Mr. H. B. McKinnon chairman of the tariff board as alternate head.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EMERGENCY POWERS BILL-STATEMENT AS TO ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief statement with regard to the resolution on the order paper concerning the extension of certain measures, as to which a request for information was made on Friday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). The resolution is to this effect:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period-
And so on. On Friday I was asked if I could supply the house promptly with a list of the numbers of the orders in council the government will ask the house to extend. I am doing that today. An office consolidation of these orders in council has been prepared. It is not in final form for distribution to hon. members, but I have a few galley proofs, of which I can send one copy to the leader of each of the parties and groups in the house, and I will lay one copy on the table so any hon. members who wish to get information as to the orders in council the government will ask the house to extend will be in possession of that informa-

Business of the House
tion as of this date, even though the resolution may not come before the house for a few days yet.
It will be appreciated that this procedure is somewhat irregular and perhaps should not be resorted to without the consent of the house, but I anticipate there will be no difficulty in getting that consent. After all, these orders in council are now the law of the land, and I think have all been either tabled or must be tabled very shortly. The statement I am making now simply amounts to this, that the government will seek extension of these orders in council for a limited period.
I think I should go further and make one fact clear; that the government is not asking for any extension whatever of powers to legislate by orders in council. The extension that is being asked is not of powers but of measures. It is proposed to append to the bill which will be placed before the house a list of these orders in council. They will be subject to revocation by the governor in council, but they will not be subject to amendment or extension by the governor in council. Where disposition of the matter otherwise than on those principles is required, legislation is being brought before the house. The principle upon which these orders in council were selected was that where measures in the judgment of the government need to be continued for a limited period of uncertain duration, the sensible thing seemed to be to do it by an extension of the orders themselves rather than by carrying them into a relatively large number of statutes. Where, however, the period required is longer, and the subject matter is one which in ordinary times is within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament, separate bills are being introduced.
I should say that among these orders in council are three which are in a different category from the rest-those relating to the veterans' preference, old age pensions and what is often referred to as the national labour code. Those orders in council will appear in the schedule to the act to be placed before the house only because legislation which is to be introduced this session relating to all three matters cannot, for various reasons which I need not give now, reasonably be expected to be introduced in time to be passed before March 31. For instance, in regard to the national labour code, negotiations are taking place with the provinces and there will need to be concurrent legislation in the provinces. In the matter of old age pensions, negotiations with the provinces in regard to the tax agreements are going on; and as to the third order in council I mentioned, con-83166- 17J
cerning the veterans' preference, legislation will be introduced this session but only after the matter has been fully discussed by a committee of this house. Therefore those orders in council are being placed in the list of measures to appear in the schedule to the act only because legislation with regard to them cannot reasonably be expected to be enacted before March 31. It is the hope of the government that the legislation on all the other matters which continue the principle of certain orders in council, and this legislation itself which will be called the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, will be passed by March 31; but of course that means a large amount of work for the house.
I should say that this list of orders in council, the numbers of which are found in the document I am going to table and distribute to the leaders of the other parties and groups in the house, may not be entirely in final form for this reason: that something as to what it contains may depend upon the disposition which the house makes of the legislation that is being placed before it. We are going to have about fifteen bills, and we have no assurance as to what the house will do with them; therefore what goes in this schedule may to some extent depend upon the disposition made of those bills.
The number of orders in council contained in this schedule will be about fifty-five. Not very 'long ago, of course, there were some thousands of orders in council, but a great many have lapsed, have become spent, have been rescinded, are being dropped or will be allowed to expire before March 31; and the number has been reduced progressively until it is expected that only a very small number will be appended to this bill.
Though it would be far more regular to convey this information to the house on the resolution or on first reading of the bill, I think possibly I should say also that we propose that the measures to be continued should remain in force until the 31st day of December, 1947, if parliament meets during November or December, 1947; but if parliament does not so meet, on the sixtieth day after parliament first meets during the year 1948, or on the 31st day of March, 1948, whichever date is the earlier, provided that if at any time while the act is in force addresses are presented to the governor general by the Senate and House of Commons respectively praying that the act should be continued in force for a further period, not in any case exceeding one year from the time at which it would otherwise expire, and the governor in council so orders, the act will continue in force for that further period.

Business of the House

When I say the government is asking that these measures be continued until that date, I mean continued subject to the power of revocation at any time, in whole or in part; and I have no doubt that just as orders in council have been rescinded from time to time in the past, so they will continue to be rescinded from time to time as the necessity for them ceases to exist; but the period of the bill is the period I have mentioned.
I think possibly that gives all the information necessary to enable hon. members to understand these office consolidations which, as I say, are merely galley proofs and not in final form, but which I wanted to give the house at the earliest possible moment so that hon. members would have the maximum notice of this legislation which, needless to say, has to be passed within a limited time.

In connection with the questions asked by the hon. members for Cape Breton South and Halifax, I wish to table order in council P.C. 302 passed on January 30, 1947. It will be observed that this order in counci' has two main objectives.
The first objective is to meet a situation brought about by the termination of control of wages by the dominion. While wage control was in effect, the subject of wages was not one that was open to the usual collective bargaining procedures between workers and management. Since wage rates had to be fixed

by the appropriate war labour board up to November 30 last, P.C. 1003, the wartime labour relations regulations, providing for compulsory collective bargaining within dominion jurisdiction exempted the whole field of wage rates from the collective bargaining contemplated by the regulations. The present order in council now amends P.C. 1003 in such manner as to include the subject of wages among the other subjects open to free collective bargaining between employer and employees. The new order in council makes the changes in P.C. 1003 needed to meet this changed situation.
The second objective of the present order is to consolidate P.C. 4020 into P.C. 1003. P.C. 4020, passed June 6, 1941, was the order in council providing for the appointment of industrial disputes inquiry commissions to investigate disputes or differences between employers and employees, and also complaints of discrimination for union activity, and to report to the Minister of Labour. It is felt that at this time it is advantageous to consolidate where possible all existing procedures in relation to the investigation and conciliation of industrial disputes into a single instrument, namely, P.C. 1003.
The order also provides for the repeal effective March 31 next of schedule A to the regulations. This has the effect of returning to the provinces as of that date jurisdiction over certain industries enumerated in the schedule and described as war industry.

subtopic: CLOSING OF PRINCE ALBERT TRAINING CENTRE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CLOSING OF PRINCE ALBERT TRAINING CENTRE
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs in connection with a matter to which I referred the other day, namely, the projected closing of the vocational training school in Prince Albert. I have had communications from the mayor and council of Prince Albert in regard to the matter, inquiring whether the instructions to close the school came from, the provincial government endeavouring to place responsibility on the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): May I refer my hon. friend to my colleague the Minister of Labour?

subtopic: CLOSING OF PRINCE ALBERT TRAINING CENTRE
speechtext:
By the very nature of things there is a substantial reduction in the number of veterans enrolling for training, and of course it is important also to reduce the expenditures of public money. These considerations have made it necessary for the Dominion Department of Labour, acting in cooperation with the Department of Veterans Affairs, to close some veterans' training centres entirely and to close individual classes in other centres. This reduction will continue throughout the summer.
All prematriculation classes will close by September except for a few special centres, possibly one in each province, to take care of disability and other special individual cases whose enrolment was unavoidably dfelayed. The Prince Albert prematriculation class, with a present enrolment of about sixty, will finish on March 31, and arrangements for its closing have been made by our regional director. By that date most of the present group will have completed their courses.
In the vocational classes of Prince Albert, farm mechanics and agricultural classes are of a fixed length and will terminate on March 31. The sheet metal class, which has only one student, will terminate at the same time. The classes in carpentry, brick-laying, motor mechanics, welding and machine shop will

continue until about June 30, when the majority of the present students, about sixty in number, will have finished their courses.
It is expected that the whole centre at Prince Albert will therefore close about the end of June.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME OF APPLICATION FOR REFUND

speechtext:
Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Customs Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-No refund for alleged inferiority or deficiency.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME OF APPLICATION FOR REFUND
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement on this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME OF APPLICATION FOR REFUND
speechtext:
The amendment to this bill is simple. Under section 124 of the Customs Act it is provided that:
No refund of duty shall be allowed because of any alleged inferiority or deficiency in quantity of goods imported and entered, and which have passed into the custody of the importer under permit of the collector, or because of the omission in the invoice of any trade discount, or other matter or thing, which might have the effect of reducing the quantity or value of such goods for duty, unless the same has been reported to the collector within fourteen (lays . . .
Under an order in council, P.C. 72/1280, passed on the 17th of February, 1943, to meet conditions as they existed at that time on account of the increased importation of goods, particularly war material, the period was extended from fourteen to thirty days in which the importer could make a claim for a refund or a remission of duties paid. That has worked so satisfactorily that upon the request of importers it has been decided to have this bill passed to extend the period to thirty days, as it was during the period of the war. It is merely a matter of convenience to business men in the country that they should have the extended time. That is the only change in the bill. We have been carrying on that practice under an order in council which, as hon. gentlemen know, will naturally cease to exist at the end of March of this year. It has been such a convenience to the importing public that we wish to extend it in statute form from fourteen to thirty days.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS

speechtext:
Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Militia Pension Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-When man promoted to rank of acting warrant officer deemed to be a man and not an officer.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
Does this amendment
apply only to warrant officers of the Royal Canadian Navy?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: That is correct; it applies to a limited group which we believe amounts to just fifteen officers. It is designed to protect the rights which we gave them during the war by order in council and which we should like to see them have. It improves their position and gives them the option of being considered either as men or as officers for the purpose of pension.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: If that is so would it not be advisable to say, "warrant officers of the Royal Canadian Navy"? There is a rank of warrant officers both in the army and in the air force. If this is designed particularly to apply to warrant officers of the Royal Canadian Navy, I suggest that it might be advisable to include that actually in the bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: To put that in the bill would not add or subtract anything from it. The words are unnecessary. The only acting warrant officers affected are in the navy and it would not help the position to include the limiting words.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
Are there not acting warrant officers in the army? Have there not been acting warrant officers in the army and in the Royal Canadian Air Force? If it is designed only for the small group in the Royal Canadian Navy-and I have no issue with the principle behind the amendment- I submit that it would make it clearer, if 83166-18
you want to limit it to the Royal Canadian Navy, to add the words "Royal Canadian Navy."

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: There is no objection to having those words in, but they do not add anything. They are unnecessary. If we can get along without them, why not?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: How will you get along without them? Without them, how do they apply only to the navy? If the minister could explain that it would remove our doubts.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I do not know of any acting warrant officers of the permanent force in the army who are promoted in this way and might come under these provisions, but if there are they should have the same advantage.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: It does not apply only to the navy but to all the services.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: As the bill is drafted it would apply to all the services if there were any, but I am informed that there are only naval ranks affected.

Section agreed to.
On section 2.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Do these provisions apply to cadets of the Royal Military College and naval cadets of Royal Roads? I ask that question because there was a group of young men who went through the Royal Military College during the first two years of the last war and who went in under special conditions. Their parents were asked to sign an agreement that they would enter the army. Later on, these particular young men, it has been found, were not made eligible for certain of the war gratuities. Their service in the Royal Military College does not count towards earning them the gratuity. Young men going through the universities of Canada, serving in the officers training corps of these universities, were eligible for these particular gratuities, and, I want to make certain that cadets of the Royal Military College, or young men going through the Royal Military College during the years 1939, 1940 and perhaps 1941, will be eligible for the benefits indicated here. I am not quite certain that cadets of the Royal Military College and possibly naval cadets of Royal Roads are considered as part of the reserve forces of the country.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
If the cadets at either Royal Roads or the Royal Military College were members of the non-permanent active militia, then their service would count. If they were not members of the non-permanent

Militia Pension Act

active militia their service would not count because the provision is limited to members of the non-permanent active militia.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Then I submit that young men who have given up their time to serve the Royal Military College or the naval college at Royal Roads should be included in this and should be classified in the same way as young men who were serving in the C.O.T.C. of the various universities. One has given up a portion of his time and the other has given up all his time to preparation for the service of his country, and I should like to see that provision definitely added there.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: The purpose of the provision is to enable officers and men of the permanent force, who served in the non-oermanent active militia, to count one quarter of that service for pension purposes after -,hey have served the appropriate length of ;ime in the permanent force to qualify for such pension. The provision does not cover men at the universities or at the Royal Military College or Royal Roads unless they are members of the non-permanent active militia. In the latter event this service would count. If they were members of the nonpermanent active militia their service for pension calculation would include one-fourth of their service in the non-permanent force.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Can the minister say whether a member of the Canadian officers training corps, university contingent, is a member of the non-permanent militia?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: My recollection is that they would all be members of the non-permanent active militia. They take an oath of attestation, That is my impression.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
I think the minister is
correct. Now, will he say whether a cadet at the Royal Military College is or is not.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Some of them may be, but as a rule they are not, because they do not become attested on entrance into the Royal Military College. They are not liable to service.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Is it not a fact that a lad joining the Royal Military College who has held a commission or has been a member of a non-permanent militia unit has to resign his commission or his membership in the unit on joining the Royal Military College? That was a condition which existed, before the war. I cannot say whether it has been changed,

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I do not think there has been any change, but the Royal Military College has not been in operation for its ordinary peacetime purposes since 1940.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: The point I am trying to make is this. The cadet at the Royal Military College is not a member of the reserve army or the non-permanent militia.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: And I am suggesting that he should be treated as such for the benefits included in this particular act, because he has given more time than a young man who is in the university, in C.O.T.C., and therefore a member of the reserve army, to preparation for his military services afterwards, and surely that time should count to his benefit just as much as the time that is put in by the young man in university.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I do not think it is a question of time. The fact is that the man attending Royal Military College and Royal Roads is not liable to military service. He is not a soldier or a sailor.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Might I ask the minister about how many people this section will apply to? He told us that the first section applied to about fifteen.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Is the number in this section as limited as that? Has he any idea of the number?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: The effect of this section is to give the men to whom it applies an option under the following section, and we do not know how many will take that option. Of course, this is intended to benefit the men, but it removes a doubt as to a date. It extends the benefit rather than limits it.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
I should like to revert to this question in connection with the Royal Military College. While it is admitted that the cadet at the Royal Military College is not or was not a member of the forces while he was serving as a cadet, what is being requested is that, if he subsequently joins either the non-permanent or the permanent force, his time at the Royal Military College will be allowed to count in the same way as is done with regard to the man who attended the officers training corps at university. That is all that is being asked. Unfortunately, an amendment to this effect, which would involve an expenditure of public funds, would be out of order. We should like to crystallize our suggestion in the form of an amendment but are unfortunately not able to do so. In order that the matter may not be

Militia Pension Act
allowed to die, I would ask that the minister say whether that particular aspect had occurred to him, and if not whether he does not think it is perhaps fair to have the cadets put in the same position?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: This has been considered, and we simply cannot see on what principle the provisions should be extended to people who were not in fact in the service during the period. They are neither soldiers nor sailors. They are not members of the non-permanent active militia. Why this benefit should subsequently be retroactively extended to them, we cannot see.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Is it a fact that the old regulations for the Royal Military College enabled a cadet who went into the permanent force to count his service at the Royal Military College toward pension after he was eighteen years of age? That is a condition which, to the best of my recollection, existed up to 1939.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: No. I want an answer to that question, please.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I will get an answer for the hon. gentleman. The answer will be here in a minute. I am informed, Mr. Chairman, the situation is as I have stated it with regard to R.M.C. With regard to naval cadets I understand it is possible that service might have counted while still in the naval college at ages subsequent to eighteen, but I am still trying to obtain that information for my hon. friend, and I shall be very glad to give it to him. In our submission, however, the test here is whether or not the soldier, sailor or airman is in one of the forces, in order to obtain the benefit of this service in the non-permanent active militia or the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve or the air force auxiliary, in order to have that count for his pension. To adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend would represent a substantial change in a provision which has been in effect for some years, which was in effect throughout the war and which of course has formed part of the understanding of these people as to their terms of service. So we submit that the provision should be left as it is, subject to the one change proposed in this bill, which makes it clear that a man who was in the active army at the 1st April, 1946, can exercise the option provided that he does so up to March 31, 1948.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
I am sorry I was not in the committee when this matter arose, but, as I understand it, the minister is saying that people who attended the Royal Military College are not entitled to have that period 83166-18J
taken into consideration for pension on the ground that they were not serving in the forces when, they were at that institution. Is that a correct understanding of what the minister says?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: That is correct,

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
In the first place, I think all hon. members will be aware that Royal Military College, as it wa9 constituted before the war, gave a completely military course of training in military matters, a course longer and much more exacting than that given in the militia or the C.O.T.C. or the reserves of the air force or the navy. It would be enough to surprise me to find the minister taking this stand, but I am much more surprised to hear him say that cadets at the Royal Military College are not in the forces. I just happen to have in my hand the Royal Military College Act, which is chapter 131 of the revise^ statutes of Canada. Section 13 reads:
Every person who enters upon a course of instruction in the college shall sign a roll of entry and shall be thenceforward for the period of his pupilage, subject to the King's Rules and Regulations, the Army Act, and to all other rules and regulations to which His Majesty's troops are subject.
So during his four years of service, whether he is at the college or not, whether he is in uniform or not, he is subject to the Army Act and the rules respecting His Majesty's forces. How such a person could not be in the forces, while a member of the non-permanent active militia, who is subject to the Army Act only at such times as be is in uniform or is proceeding to or is at a place of parade, is in the forces, is quite beyond my understanding. I am sure the minister must be mistaken, and before going on I would ask him to reconsider the question of whether or not these cadets were in the forces. From what I have before me, I am quite satisfied that they were.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: The situation is as I have described it. Gentlemen attending the Royal Military College and Royal Roads are not members of the non-permanent active militia, nor are they members of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve or the air force auxiliary. They are not active force; they are not permanent force, and) they are not reserve force. They are not members of the forces, though, as the hon. member has said, while at the college they are subject to military law. They are not liable to service; that is the test.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
Is the minister able to answer my question as to whether cadets, when reaching the age of eighteen, previously
2fiS
Militia Pension Act

were able to count their service at the Royal Military College toward their pension in the permanent force?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I am informed that is not the case, but I am having that information checked again. I am informed they only count their service from the time they are in fact attested.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: You mean when they are granted commissions, after leaving the college?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: If the minister is in doubt as to the accuracy of his information, as I am in doubt, will he let this section stand until he has checked it?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I am in the hands of the committee, Mr. Chairman, but even if the information is incorrect-though I am sure it is correct-it would not alter the attitude we take, which is that cadets at Royal Military College or Royal Roads are not in the forces. They are not liable to service, and therefore attendance at these places should not count for pension purposes. I shall be glad to get my hon. friend the information, in any event, and give him full particulars; but I think this section should be carried.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I should like to come back to the question asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, as to the maximum number of officers, non-commissioned officers and men who will be affected by this provision.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Any officer, non-commissioned officer or man who was enlisted in the permanent force on or before the 1st day of April, 1946, and who elects to come under part V before March 31, 1948, may have the advantage of this provision.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: But how many are affected? That is what I want to get. How many people in the service today can elect to come under this section?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: All those who were in the permanent force on or before April 1, 1946, and who make an election before the 31st March, 1948. as well as all those who were enlisted in the permanent force of Canada on and after April 1, 1946. That might be a very substantial proportion of those in the permanent forces today. They may make this election. We do not know how many will do so. The number covered by the amendment will be much smaller.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: But how many men are there in the service who served in the militia, the air force auxiliary or the naval reserve and can elect to come under this section of the act? You must have that figure.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Anyone in the permanent force on April 1, 1946, and who makes the election before the 31st March, 1948, who had service in the non-permanent active militia before entering the permanent force may have the advantage of this provision. We do not know how many people there are in the permanent force who had service before in the non-permanent militia.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Surely that information is available in the department?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I suppose it could be traced through the attestation papers.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I think we should have it. We are being asked to vote on something which affects a great many people, and I think we should have the information as to how many people who are in the permanent force of today come under this section of the act.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: If we were taking away the rights of any people, then I would think the hon. member's point was well taken, but we are merely making a drafting correction in a provision which already exists and therefore it seems to me the information is not relevant.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
I listened attentively
to the arguments advanced by hon. members on this side. Perhaps I am not as well posted as they on this matter, but I feel that the history and tradition of the Royal Military College is such that we do not want to make any error at this time and possibly create discrimination. I think the minister should let this stand for the time being. There are some of us who come from parts of the country from which many Royal Military College students have come. These boys have served with great distinction, and I do not think this thing should be rushed through at the present time with the possibility of causing discrimination. I consider the presentations of the hon. members to my left extremely well taken and I suggest that the minister not try to rush this thing through.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
I am sure hon. members will appreciate that all this amendment seeks to do is to make a textual alteration in the provisions of the act which was enacted at the last session of parliament. Section 2 of this bill would have the effect of leaving out any person appointed to or enlisted in the forces on or before April 1, 1946, who elects to come under part V before the 31st March, 1948. Upon an examination of the law as it had been in effect during this last year, it was found that it should be made clear that not only did those people have who enlisted later come under the provisions of this part, but

Canada Grain Act
also those who were already in and exercised their right of election to come under this part before March 31, 1948. This change is proposed to make that clear. It does not take away anyone's rights. It makes it clear that they have the rights which parliament intended to give them at the last session.
Mr. PEARKE8:	I fully appreciate that,
but there is still the question of that certain group of young men who attended special courses during the first two years of the war at the Royal Military College. Their parents signed undertakings that at the conclusion of those courses they would go into the services. While there, those young men took the oaths which were read out to them and were attested in the manner described by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt). To all intents and purposes they were in the service at that time. I contend that they were more in the service than the young man who was attending university and also taking training in the C.O.T.C. The young men taking these particular courses were serving under conditions quite different from anything which had occurred before, and I suggest that they were overlooked. I am just trying to protect their interests. I am thinking only of those young men who joined the services after passing their courses. I do not know how many, but there are likely some who have elected to stay on in the permanent force. I feel that these young men should be treated the same as the other young Canadians who were attending universities and training in the C.O.T.C.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Those young men were not in fact liable for service and they were not within the classes intended to be covered. Consequently they were not covered by the legislation.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: If a young man was attending Royal Military College for a year after war broke out and he is to be allowed only one-quarter of that year toward his pension, then it does not seem to me it amounts to a great deal. However, if it is extended to students who were at the college for four years it would make a considerable difference. The minister has said that these students were not liable for service and that is one reason he gives for the position that has been taken. However, I submit that they were liable to service in a limited sense. Were they not obliged to undertake to join a unit when they graduated from the Royal Military College? If they were required to do that, then they were liable for service. Perhaps they were not liable when they were at the Royal Military College but they were obligated to serve when they graduated.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
There is another bill ready and I will agree to allow this one to stand for a moment.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE PROVISIONS OF ORDERS IN COUNCIL

speechtext: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Canada Grain Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE PROVISIONS OF ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Are we not going to have a statement from the minister with respect to this bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE PROVISIONS OF ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I have very little to add to the statement I made on the first reading of the bill, although I might enlarge on it a little. The amendments cover four points. First, there is an extension of the requirements of insurance coverage in eastern elevators as there has been heretofore in western elevators.
Another amendment is the establishment of permanent bases of grades which had been developed during the war for oil seeds and peas.
Section, 4 seeks the continuation of authority to the governor in council to postpone the annual weigh-over of grain in elevators to meet situations arising from storage congestion, transportation difficulties or other tie-ups. This power was given during the war to meet emergencies and' is regarded as necessary to permit reasonable flexibility in future operations.
The transfer of carloading authority is a provision which speaks for itself and one which should have been in the act right along, to ensure the equitable distribution of cars at country elevators.
In committee I am prepared to make a more complete statement on each section as we reach it.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCORPORATE PROVISIONS OF ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I asked the minister to make a statement at this time was this: I was going to ask him whether he would consent to having this bill go to the committee on agriculture.
He has outlined: that there are four points in this measure. With respect to three of them I think there will be no serious objection; certainly we have none. With respect to [DOT] the other, there is some question in our minds whether it should be passed without fuller con-
Canada Grain Act

sideration. That is the amendment to give the board power to postpone the weigh-over in the elevators. I think that is the important section, section 4 on page 2 of the bill, which would- amend section 138 of the Canada Grain Act. Section 138 of the Canada Grain Act imposes on the board the duty of weighing-over the grain contained in every terminal elevator within specified periods. During the war, under the wide powers that were given the government, that requirement was suspended, and the government now asks that this wartime procedure be continued. I am raising some question as to the propriety of parliament granting that power. The original legislation was designed to prevent malpractices or the possibility of certain malpractices ot the misuse of grain so stored in these elevators.
The reason given in the explanatory note for the amendment is that in times of acute storage congestion it may not be possible to carry out this requirement. But that condition does not obtain now. It probably did obtain during the war and may obtain again, but it does not obtain now, and my contention is that we should not amend the old section to give the board power to omit or defer a weigh-over without -being assured- that that is the wise course to follow. When in his opinion the public interest so requires the minister may by regulation provide that only feeding stuffs of the kind or composition specified . . .
My understanding is that under the section previously in the act the minister was required to register these particular feeding stuffs if application was made, and different requirements were set out. But a practice grew up whereby a company manufacturing feeding stuffs simply brought in another, slightly different form of the feeding stuff, a slightly different mixture, in order to put it on the market as another grade of feed stuff and thus require another price for it, putting it into competition with commodities already being sold. During the war it was declared that there was not sufficient difference between many of these registered feeds for which registration was being asked to warrant the mixtures being put on the market under a different brand. maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: Will the minister explain these amendments?

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: The Inspection and Sale Act, 1938, makes provision for grading and maintaining the standards of certain products, and part I covers binder twine. During the war we sold considerable flax fibre and tow to the British government and during that time we were asked to grade the flax fibre and tow being sold to the British government. As a result of the experiences gained, it is considered, by both the producers and the trade, that it would be a good thing to have that provision put in this act. The bill provides that we may grade fibre flax and tow which may be sold from time to time and these provisions are put in as part IA, the sections being numbered 12A, 12B and so on.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: Is any great quantity of flax being produced in Canada? I understood the minister to say that most of it was going to Great Britain; is that still the case?

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext:
In the first year of the war, 1939-40, there were 8,306 acres of land in Canada engaged in the growing of fibre flax. That was increased in the first year of the war to 20,000 acres. In 1941-42 the acreage was increased to 44,000, and in 1942-43, to 47,000. From 1942-43 down to the present there has been a reduction in acreage. In 1943-44 the acreage was down to 33,000, and there was a slight increase in 1944-45 to 38,000 acres. In 1945-46 it was down to 21,000 acres. Last year, largely owing to the fact that the season was late and those who seed flax do not like to take chances on late seeding, the total acreage was down to 15,762 acres.
It is expected that the acreage will go up this year, probably back to about 21,000 acres. It is not likely that it will increase much beyond that. The amount secured for the flax in the different years ranged from $837,000 in 1939-40 to $2,25 ,000 in 1943-44, and: this despite the fact that that was not the highest year as far as total acreage was concerned. However, the price was higher in that year. The reductions in the years following are partly due to the fact that there has been a
decrease in the amount offered for the flax. Perhaps I might give the prices, which are as follows:

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: If my memory serves me correctly, during the last war there was a large increase in the production of flax fibres in Canada and this was a profitable business for both the farmers and the merchants. However, at the close of the war production began to decline, largely on account of lower prices as well as certain other factors. The result was that the flax business in Canada went out of existence entirely. I am just wondering whether something similar might not happen now. No doubt the needs of the war were responsible for the increase in flax production as well as the good: prices being offered by the British government, but I hope nothing will be done by the Department of Agriculture to induce people to go into the flax business. After the last war many men lost everything they had in the flax business.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext:
I wish to express my appreciation for the words just uttered by the hon. member who, I understand, is the
Inspection and Sale Act

official agricultural critic of the official opposition. He has just expressed the view which we hold. At the beginning of the war quite a number of people came to Canada from some of the European countries and they were ardent promoters of the production of flax. On every occasion when a delegation came to us, sometimes headed by some of these people, we gave exactly the warning which has just been given by the hon. member for Haldimand, namely, that the experience of the first war was that the flax which we could produce in this country, and produce successfully, was required in great quantities during that war, but dropped very rapidly following the war. I think the acreage was increased from around the smaller acreage we had in this last war up to about 40,000 acres; then after the war, it dropped to 10,000 or 12,000 acres. As has been stated, a considerable number of people lost money in attempting to stay in the business too long. When we were approached in 1943 or 1944 to increase the price from fifty-five to sixty-three cents we inquired why sixty-three cents was suggested. It was stated that persons here who were familiar with the production of flax and were on land suitable for flax growing could produce flax for fifty-five cents or even less, but that if persons who were not on the best flax land and had had no experience in flax growing were to be induced to go into flax growing we would have to pay up to sixty-three cents. We refused to go up to sixty-three cents or to pay any subsidy that would make that price possible. We advised the farmers to be careful in proceeding to get into flax growing in a big way if their land was better suited to something else, and that had something to do with the reduction in acreage beginning back in 1943. We are not urging them to increase the present acreage, although I would not be surprised, if conditions are favourable in the spring, if some who got partly out of flax last year went back into it.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext:
Was any amount specified in
the agreement with Great Britain?

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: The agreement involves a substantial price reduction which the British board of trade claims was justified in order to bring the price being paid for Canadian flax into line with prices paid for comparable quantities from other empire sources. It was suggested that they would take all we could produce at that price on the acreage we then had, but there was no inducement to cultivate any larger acreage than was then available. In fact the considerable reduction in price would indicate that they were not anxious to have the acreage increased this year.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: With regard to the inspection certificate mentioned in paragraph (c), will the inspection certificates issued by the officers of the department be recognized by buyers from abroad? I mention that because, during the war when the British buyers were here, complaints were made by flax growers in the district I have the honour to represent that the British inspectors were too exacting in their requirements. Now that we are to continue our inspection, I wonder if the Canadian inspection certificate will be recognized by buyers from other countries.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: Some difficulty was experienced about the middle of the war when the price was increased and an inspection was required. The British sent an inspector over who passed upon flax and flax fibre before it was finally accepted. My memory is that, after some misunderstandings and some discussions between our own people and the British, the Canadian inspections were almost invariably accepted, and I think there is an understanding now between the British and ourselves which will result in standards established by our certificates being acceptable to the British.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: Certain people from certain countries in Europe came here and urged us to go into production of flax fibre. I believe those people had linen mills in certain countries in Europe, and I was wondering if the minister could indicate whether these people showed any inclination to establish branches of their mills in Canada to process our fibre flax in this country.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: The persons I was referring to specifically were in the business in this country. Whether they have gone back to their own countries or not I am not in a position to say, but I do not think they have; I think they are still here. They came over here in the early part of the war, after having been in the same business on the continent of Europe, and they established themselves in the business here and were quite active in it. Naturally they were anxious to get a greater acreage of flax produced so that they would have greater quantities to handle. I must say this for them, that immediately we made the suggestions I have just mentioned to the committee, they ceased to advocate an increased acreage for flax production in this country, and they went on to handle the product that was here.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext:
They have not shown any intention of establishing branch factories in this country?

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
speechtext: I would not want to be too certain about that. If they did not establish plants of their own, they were engaged by others who had plants.

speechtext:
This is one of the first of the bills incorporating orders in council passed in wartime. Looking over some of the provisions of this bill, I notice that the minister has power to make regulations prescribing standards of grade, class or quality for flax fibre and the names or marks that may be used to designate such grade, class or quality; also to provide for the inspection, grading and labelling of flax fibre, and generally for carrying into effect any of the purposes or provisions of part I of the bill. Most of these
powers in almost identical terms were to be found in the Natural Products Marketing Act, which became law during the Bennett administration and which was submitted to the supreme court after the defeat of that administration. Later on, the references were taken to the privy council where the Natural Products Marketing Act was declared ultra vires. As I understand the argument in the privy council, it was held that the act purported to control not only export and interprovincial trade but also trade within a province. Have these particular amendments been submitted to the law officers of the crown, and if so will the minister give the committee the benefit of the opinions they gave as to whether or not these sections are within the power of parliament?

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES

The bill has been submitted to the law officers of the Department of Justice. I think section 12(b) answers the question. It reads as follows:
No person shall export any flax fibre unless it is inspected, graded, marked or designated, and labelled in accordance with the regulations made under this part.
It is only a product that has been exported which must be brought under this act.

maintopic: INSPECTION AND GRADING OF FLAX FIBRES
