subtopic: INGREDIENTS ENTERING INTO PRODUCTION- PROPERTIES OF FERTILIZERS

speechtext: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Fertilizers Act.

subtopic: INGREDIENTS ENTERING INTO PRODUCTION- PROPERTIES OF FERTILIZERS
speechtext:
Because of the ramifications of fertilizer products I should like to draw to the attention
Fertilizers Act

not only of the Minister of Agriculture but of all hon. members the situation in regard to fertilizer, its production, distribution and price. I wish to draw attention to this fact. I think all hon. members will agree that from the short point of view we want immediate all-out production in Canada. Fertilizer applied to our land today in every field of agriculture will increase production. My second point is that from the long point of view we have in the past exploited this great resource of our country, our land, to the extent that unless we make provision so that farmers can use fertilizers on their soil we are going to face decreased production, and also find that we are mining out our land of those precious elements which can be replaced only by various types of fertilizer.
I hold in my hand a publication put out by Mr. F. A. McGregor entitled "Canada and the International Cartels". The first cartel or monopoly which he deals with in this pamphlet is fertilizer. I do not know whether the commissioner places the most importance on that or not, but at any rate we find that in Canada today there are three main constituents in the mixture of fertilizers, namely, potash, nitrogen and phosphorus.
I should like to follow closely the development of the fertilizer business in Canada because, in spite of all the ramifications which it may have in the international picture, here in Canada the Canadian people and the farmers generally are much concerned about it. Prior to the great war, the potash industry was largely controlled within the German empire by a German syndicate. With the restoration, after the first great war. of Alsace-Lorraine to France we find that the Alsatian deposits came under French control. After a brief period of competition, the German and French companies got together and, under an understanding formed a cartel. The important thing is that we find that from 1924 to 1933 a uniform price was maintained throughout the world. Later on in 1932, when the Polish producers of fertilizer came into the market they started to compete with the world cartel which had been built up, and they were finally dragged into the cartel arrangement and given four per cent of the world market. In that way the cartel stopped the pressure on breaking the price of fertilizer throughout the world. This condition remained in existence until 1934 when the Russian and Spanish fertilizers came on to the world markets. During that time the Lnited States market was increasing production. The effect of this competition from the new sources of production, and the elimination of the Spanish and Russian

exporters are reflected in the prices which are given in this pamphlet by the commissioner. We find that in 1932 the price per unit of 20 pounds of potash was $0,619. That price was maintained until 1934 when there was competition; the price of the world cartel was broken, and the price was brought down to $0,300, or a little less than fifty per cent of the price established in 1932.
After these cartels got together in 1939, we find that they were once again successful in increasing the price of fertilizer until in 1939 it was $0,471.

subtopic: INGREDIENTS ENTERING INTO PRODUCTION- PROPERTIES OF FERTILIZERS
speechtext: Where was that?

subtopic: INGREDIENTS ENTERING INTO PRODUCTION- PROPERTIES OF FERTILIZERS
speechtext:
It is f.o.b. United States ports. This showed clearly that these companies entering into the cartel arrangements were able to control prices. One thing that we should note carefully is that in Canada we have no great deposits of potash which is one of the ingredients we require in our fertilizer, and therefore it is of tremendous importance to us. We find a branch of the European cartel with a selling company established in Montreal, which is the Canadian subsidiary of the great German-French cartel with headquarters in Holland. This is what the report says:
The close relationship between the cartel and the American producers of potash provided an opportunity for Canadian manufacturers and distributors of fertilizers to formulate common policies as to prices and conditions of sale.
The table I have quoted will, I believe, bear this out. One of the other chief ingredients of fertilizer is, of course, nitrogen. Prior to world war I, fifty-four per cent of the world requirement of nitrogen compounds was produced in Chile and it was a by-producf of the steel and coke industries and of other activities as well. During the war, we started in Canada to produce our own nitrogen and, by the end of the war, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company was able to manufacture a synthetic fertilizer at Trail, British Columbia. This is of extreme importance to us because, after being at the mercy of the fertilizer-producing countries of the world, we in Canada had in that crown company an opportunity of producing this material for ourselves.
My information is that the government expressly promised the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that either this or one of the other wartime plants would be kept under public ownership so that the world monopoly would not get the Canadian farmer in its grasp. The Canadian Mining and Smelting Company of British Columbia was producing

Fertilizers Act
a waste by-product going into nitrates, a product going into fertilizer. As I say, it was a by-product, and while the company was selling it to the mixers at $33 a ton the farmers were paying $44. I think the minister will agree with me that it is a waste product in the foundries of the smelting company. In fact, you have to put a price on it as a waste product. We produced in these war plants at Calgary and at Welland this product, ammonia nitrate.
I suggest that this is perhaps one of the sell-outs of the Canadian farmer on the part of the government, because here we had an opportunity of maintaining a crown-owned corporation where we could produce fertilizers for the farmers, which they must get if they are to maintain the nitrogen content of our soil. But instead of doing that, the Alberta Nitrogen Products plant and the Trail smelting company, the former costing $9,821,000 odd and the latter $5,816,217 were sold for $7,500,000, or less than half the original price of the two. They were sold at half the original cost to the Canadian taxpayers.
I contend, therefore, that we have messed things up here and that the time has come, if we wish to take with any seriousness the report of our commissioner, when we should make provision to supply our farmers at a decent price the fertilizers which they so greatly need.

subtopic: INGREDIENTS ENTERING INTO PRODUCTION- PROPERTIES OF FERTILIZERS
speechtext:
I was very much interested in the remarks made by the hon. member, but I think it is necessary to say something on the second reading of the bill as a result of what has already been said.
It is perfectly true that potash is an important ingredient of fertilizer'and that practically all the potash we used in the past came from Europe, some of it from the sources mentioned, and some from Russia.
The situation with regard to nitrates is partly as has been described. Prior to the war, we had got most of our fertilizer in western Canada from the operations of the Trail smelting plant and we did as well get a considerable part of our nitrates from another plant which is located in the Niagara peninsula. During the war it became necessary to have nitrates produced for the manufacture of explosives and one of the plants opened for that purpose was the plant at Calgary, to which reference has been made.
My understanding is that during the war nitrates were produced at Calgary at the lowest cost of any plant established anywhere. I have heard it stated on good authority, and I believe it can be substantiated, that nitrates were laid down in Halifax from
Calgary at a cost lower than from anywhere else on this continent. The plant was an efficient one and did an important job during the war. Unfortunately we do not require very much in the form of nitrates for fertilizer in western Canada. Our fertilizer mixtures require other ingredients in so far as we use fertilizer at all in the west. We are not heavy users of fertilizers.
It has been suggested that probably someone was sold out in the disposition of the plant.
I had considerable experience with it myself, and 1 would not want anyone to go away with the idea that anyone was sold out without at least having an opportunity of buying before any selling was done.
The president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture raised the question as to whether or not this plant should be sold, and they raised it first, in a very effective way, with the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who had been responsible for the establishment of the plant in the first place and for its utilization during the war. Then the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture brought the matter to the attention of the Department of Agriculture and asked us to take an interest in the matter and see whether this plant could not be put in the hands of someone other than Consolidated Smelters or any other organization that had been in the business up until then.
I went to the then Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and, without any hesitation whatsoever, he said that the plant was being put on the market and would be sold, that he invited bids on it from any source whatsoever. Not only did he agree to that, but for the greater part of a year- I have forgotten the exact period of time now, but it could be obtained from the records-he refrained from selling the plant. During that period of time, I personally took the matter up with every organization in western Canada that had money. At that time one of the very strong organizations in western Canada had a profit of seven million dollars which, I suppose, could have been utilized under certain circumstances for doing certain things. They examined into the possibilities of buying and operating the plant; other organizations examined into the possibilities of buying and operating it, and the matter was publicly discussed so that any government or anyone desiring to go intc that kind of business could have gone into it. But no one desired to do so.
I say quite candidly that the reason the government did not go into it was that we have not been advocates of that kind of thing. We have not been advocating that
Fertilizers Act

the government should go into that type of business at any time. We have been maintaining that that type of business is a legitimate business for either private or cooperative capital to be in, and we believe that kind of business will be much more efficiently operated in the interest of everyone concerned if it is carried on either through the utilization of private capital or through the utilization of capital made available by cooperatives set up by the people who desire to use the product. So we took sufficient time, by correspondence, by meeting delegations and otherwise, ki trying to interest some of these people in that plant in order that it might be operated in a manner which they might think would be in the interests of the farmer. I am not going to say that others, whether it be government or whether it be farmers' cooperatives, were unwise in not taking on this particular investment; because, as was stated by the hon. member a few moments ago, the greatest supply of the product prior to the war as well as during the first war was obtained from Chile. The only way in which that plant could be operated successfully purely for the production of fertilizer, according to the information we were able to gather, was by producing nitrates which would be marketed largely in the United States and which would be sold in competition with the product that comes from Chile. Everyone who examined into the possibilities of the plant-and that included the cooperatives in the west-came to the conclusion that it was not a good business proposition into which to put the money of his organization, and I presume that, if the western governments gave any thought to it, they probably came to the same conclusion.
The plant was eventually sold to the highest bidder and the highest bidder was Consolidated Smelters. Consolidated Smelters bought the plant, I think at the figure which was indicated by the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. McCullough) a few minutes ago, seven million and some odd thousand dollars. They have that plant now.
While I was west recently I made a number of speeches, as hon. members know, and some of them appeared in the press. But in addition to the speeches, I had the usual number of newspapermen who wanted interviews; and one of them who had an interview, afterwards published in the press a statement to the effect that I had said that Consolidated Smelters had taken this plant over and closed it up. Immediately upon seeing that item in the Vancouver Province, I telephoned the editor and told him that I could not have made any such state-
ment as that because the plant was not closed up. But the incident had its good effect, because the next day I received a telephone call from the vice-president of the company who was then in Victoria, who told me that one of the newspapers had wanted a story from him contradicting what I had said in order that they might be able to write it up. Instead of giving that, he telephoned to me to ask me what I really had said. I told him what I had said, namely, that I hoped the company was not going to close it up. He said, "Well, I can tell you quite emphatically that we have no intention of closing it up; we intend to go on and operate it." So I am pleased to know that the company which has it, Consolidated Smelters, do intend to operate it and do intend to utilize it for the purpose of making an ingredient of fertilizer to the extent that it can be disposed of and utilized.
I wanted to say that in order to indicate that the government have not thoughtlessly allowed this plant to be sold to Consolidated Smelters. They have given every opportunity possible to anyone else who desired to go into the business of producing fertilizer. We even went so far as to urge upon every farm organization that has considerable capital for other things, that they utilize some of it for that purpose; and to urge on them that, if they did not desire to utilize the capital in the present organization, they do something similar to what was done in relation to farm implements. When we were having our discussion early in the war, or just before the war, with regard1 to farm implements, many of us took the position that the proper way to deal with the question was to form a cooperative in western Canada to make farm implements available at lower costs. That kind of organization is there today. It has considerable capital. It ha9 not seen fit to manufacture, but maybe someday it will manufacture. We even suggested to the farmers in western Canada that, if the present organization were not in a position to deal with the matter, an organization be established for that purpose. All I have to say with regard to it is that we were not able to interest anyone in it; and finally, after months had gone by and every means had been exhausted for having this plant turned over to somebody out there who wanted to operate it, and it had been made known to everyone who wanted to discuss the matter and to many who did not want to discuss it, it was 3old to the only company that seemed interested, namely, Consolidated. Smelters.

speechtext:
They
operated, making fertilizer, for about six months, and did a wonderful job.

speechtext:
I am not sure about the period of a week, but I do know that in a very short time they could make in that plant all the nitrates necessary for the production of fertilizer in Canada. It is also true that the other plant located in Canada produces a very large part of the nitrates required for the production of fertilizers in eastern Canada. That is why I say one of the influencing factors in relation to some of these people about whom I have been speaking was that they found that if they operated the plant they would have to go into the United States market, where probably eighty ot ninety per cent of the product turned out-I am not sure of the percentages-would have to be sold. They no doubt thought that as farm organizations they were not inclined to invest the sum of money necessary to obtain control of that plant in order to sell nitrates in the United States.
As to the matter of terms, I have not the contract here and I would not be too definite about it, but my memory is that the option they had was at the figure which has been stated, $7,000,000 odd. I do not think they were to be permitted to buy at the highest price that might be offered, but I am speaking subject to correction. Perhaps my hon. friend knows more about the matter than I do. My memory is that they got the plant at the price indicated at the time the arrangement was entered into, but I do not think that would have prevented anyone else from bidding more had they desired to do so.

Does this give the
minister power to prescribe certain formulas for fertilizer?

speechtext: Has the department the power to compel a farmer to use a certain formula of fertilizer?

speechtext:
As far as the
Interpretation Act is concerned, it has nothing whatever to do with the relationship of the crown. In a number of cases it has been decided that the Interpretation Act does not apply to any reference to the crown, and in every case the crown is in the position where the word "may" applies to it not permissively but obligatorily. While there has been argument for years over that question, nevertheless there have been recent authorities-I believe there has been one within the last two years- wherein it has been stated that "may", applied to the crown, is invariably interpreted as "shall".
With regard to this particular section, I have the act before me, and I find that the minister is the person who enjoys all these powers and not any committee set up by the provinces. Section 10 says the minister "may". Then paragraph (i) says, "make regulations prescribing the chemical, physical or other properties." This is placing the minister, not a committee of any province, in a position of having absolute power to determine what shall be sold, where it shall be sold, and the circumstances under which it shall be sold. That is putting in the hands of the minister tremendous power uncontrolled in any way. In other words, the whole act, including the amendments that have been introduced this evening and which have already been passed, indicate a widespread advance along the way of bureaucratic control in this country. Earlier the minister received power under paragraph (f) of section 1 to demand any relevant information, as the minister may require, and I could understand his asking for that power. Then under section 3 he received the power to demand such other relevant information as may be prescribed by regulation. Those sections gave him wide powers. This section places the minister in the position of being able to determine what companies shall, in

fact, sell fertilizer if they are not selling the type of fertilizer that he deems necessary for any particular area.

After all, however desirable the aim, which is to assure that the farmer shall know the content of the fertilizer he purchases, nevertheless this goes far beyond that and says that not only shall he know, but no matter what his wishes are he shall purchase only that which the minister designates that he shall purchase. That represents a gross interference with the rights of the individual far and beyond the need of protecting his rights. I feel sure that, no matter how one looks at those other subsections in section 10 of the act as at present constituted, he will realize that never before has a minister asked the absolute power that is asked for under this particular subsection. No person shall advertise, offer, sell, expose or 'hold in possession for sale any potash salts containing more than five-tenths of one per cent of anhydrous borax, or mixed fertilizer containing more than one-tenth of one per cent of anhydrous borax, or any fertilizer containing sufficient destructive ingredients or properties which may prove harmful to plant growth when the fertilizer is used in a reasonable manner.

Then coming down to the section we are dealing with, the section preceding it provides that the minister may make regulations prescribing the methods to be used in the examination or analysis of any fertilizer for the purposes of this act. Then comes the section we are proposing to put in, and it is followed by:
The minister may make regulations for any other purpose deemed by him to be necessary for making effective the provisions of this act.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand that the object of section 2 is to recognize the preparations which a large number of men of this country gave to be prepared in the event of a war breaking out during a period of time between great war I and great war II. It covers all this personnel

Militia Pension Act
who served in the non-permanent active militia, the reserves of the navy and of the air force, including such units of the nonpermanent militia as the university contingent of the C.O.T.C. Before we adjourned, I called attention to the fact that the corps oi gentlemen cadets of the Royal Military College and the naval cadets of the Royal Naval College of Royal Roads were not included. I pointed out that the corps of gentlemen cadets at the Royal Military College had not in the past been recognized as being an integral part of the non-permanent militia of Canada. In fact, King's Rules and Regulations say that the Royal Military College is supplementary to, though not an integral part of, the permanent militia; but it is generally recognized that the training which gentlemen cadets received at the Royal Military College did fit them admirably for the service of their country when they had graduated from that college and had gone into the various units of the militia. That fact was recognized because they were given seniority over individuals entering into the permanent force from other sources, such as through the militia or graduating from the university C.O.T.C. The gentlemen cadets of the Royal Military College were given one year's seniority over those who came in from the non-permanent active militia. Furthermore, that training was recognized by the fact that the time spent at the Royal Military College wTas permitted to count toward the efficiency decoration which was awarded after so many years of service in one of the units of the militia. They were also allowed to count their service at the Royal Military College toward their promotion and toward increases of pay according to the term of years which they had served. For instance, a subaltern got a raise in pay after three years service and another raise in pay after six years service. The service that an individual had put in at the Royal Military College had always counted toward these increases in pay. My contention is that, although the Royal Military College may not be recognized as being an integral part of the non-permanent militia, there is no question about it that these young men who were at that college were there with the idea of preparing themselves for an emergency. They operated in exactly the same way as the young men who were in the non-permanent militia units preparing themselves.
It is true that the gentlemen cadets at the Royal Military College were under military discipline while there. On the outbreak of the first world war, the senior classes were at once closed and were given the opportunity, which
they at once accepted, of entering into the services of the country. Therefore it is purely a legal quibble to say that they are not a part of the militia. Their years of preparation justify them just as much as the years of preparation which the other young, men of the country put in the university C.O.T.C. for this recognition. I feel it is an oversight that the Royal Military College and the Royal Naval College, Royal Roads, have been omitted from this provision, and I am sure the minister will realize this. I hope he will agree to adding these two corps to this list.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
When the discussion of section 2 was adjourned the hon. member had asked me whether the point he was making had been considered by the government when this clause was drafted. I should point out that the clause in the bill before us makes no change whatever in the existing situation with regard to the type of service that will be counted for pension purposes. This clause, in so far as the point made by the hon. member for Nanaimo in concerned, is in the same terms as the clause that was adopted by this house last year when part V of the Militia Pension Act was enacted, and indeed a similar provision will be found in the Militia Pension Act amendments of 1928, in the Revised Statutes, 1927, chapter 133, section 8, and in 1919, and a similar clause, though not in the same words, will be found in the amendments made to the Militia Pension Act as far back as 1910 when for the first time, I think I am correct in saying, service in the non-permanent active militia was to count for past service in the permanent force for pension purposes.
I have made inquiries and find that the point put forward by my hon. friend has been advanced at various times during this whole period. It is not an oversight. This has received the most serious consideration, and it has simply been found, without derogation to the fine qualities and characteristics of the Royal Military College and Royal Roads, that they axe not "services", and the Militia Act puts pension on the basis of "service". The basis on which pension is calculated is service in one of the armed forces of Canada, and I should point out that section 42, subsection 1, provides that not only must the service in the non-permanent active militia- the reserve as we call it now-be in a unit of the non-permanent active militia, but in order to count for your pension when you are in the active army, the service must have been with the army; and in order to count for your pension with the navy, the service must have been with the naval reserve, and similarly with the air force.

speechtext:
After the close of great
war I, in order to encourage those officers who had been in the non-permanent militia to enter into the permanent force, they were allowed to count their pensionable service in the nonpermanent militia as two years, or one-half of the time.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: May I ask why that has been changed to one-quarter now? Surely we want to encourage those men who were in the non-permanent militia before world war II to go into what is to be a largely increased active army. I should like to know what the point is in reducing the amount of benefit from one-half to one-quarter?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: That change was made last year by this house when it enacted part V of the act. The purpose of part V was to provide a system of pensions for the permanent force, or the active army, as we now call it. It would be similar in its provision to that for the civil service and the other services of Canada. I think in working it out it will be found that, by and large, the provisions regarding pensions that are now to be found in part V are fair and generous. But the point of all this is that anyone who enlisted and was a member of the permanent force prior to March 31, 1946, can either stay under the old pension provisions or, if he prefers and so elects by March 31, 1948, he can come under the new pension provisions, part V. The purpose of this amendment that we are putting before the house today is just to do one thing, namely, to make it clear that he has that election, that he has the choice either to stay under the old provisions or to come in under the new ones. We do not know how many men will come under the new provisions, but we imagine a considerable proportion of them will do so.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I am afraid the minister has not quite answered my question. I asked what the point was of reducing it from one-half to one-quarter.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
It was considered that
part V, as it was drafted as a whole, provided a fair pension plan and that a quarter was a fair period of time to allow in respect of the

non-permanent active service. I think I should also point out that this is not free, that if a man wishes to avail himself of the service, he will have to make a contribution which will be related to the benefit to be obtained. Consequently this is not nearly as serious as it might be thought to ibe by hon. members who are not quite as familiar with the provisions as others. This was, as I say, adopted last year. One-quarter was thought to be a fair amount, having regard to the part-time nature of the non-permanent active militia and the working reserve. Taken together with the other provisions, it was considered to be a generous one.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Would the minister explain why this section is so restrictive? A man in the permanent force of the army must have served with the militia and the militia only. A man in the air force must have served in the air force auxiliary and the same thing is true of the navy. Our whole move today is to have the service regarded as one service. As far as the air force is concerned, particularly before the war I know it was very difficult for a young lad who was keen to serve, to get into the auxiliary air force. One reason for that was that there wore so few units. Even in places like Vancouver, where there was a unit, it was very difficult for a young man who was keen to serve in the non-permanent force to get into the auxiliary air force. As a consequence, a great number of them joined the militia, which they could do. If these men should stay on in the permanent air force, having joined the air force, it seems unfair to me that their militia time before the war should not be counted on their pension plan.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: The answer to the hon. member's question is this. The idea has been to count only service in the reserve of the arm of the service in which the man serves in the permanent force. That was deliberately done. It was made restrictive. It has been so since 1910. There is no change in it. It is considered to be a fair provision.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: We did not have an air force in 1910.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: It was reenacted in 1940 and in 1946; it received consideration on all those occasions, and no reason to change it has been found.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
The very fact that it was good in 1910 definitely does not make it good today. In 1910, for example, we had no air force; and the one lesson which we should have learned out of 83166-20
this war is the need of having just one armed service for Canada. It certainly does seem ridiculous deliberately to exclude lads who did give the best sort of non-permanent service before the war, simply because they are not now in the little pigeonhole they were in before. Therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, I should like to move in amendment that in paragraphs (A), (B) and (C) the last words "in respect of army personnel", "in respect of air force personnel" and "in respect of naval personnel" be deleted. The effect of that will be that a man who served in any branch of the non-permanent forces can get one-quarter of the time spent in any branch of the permanent forces.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I regret having to do so, but I would point out that this clause as it stands and as amended, if the amendment were to carry, would impose a charge on the treasury'; and consequently I submit that it is out of order.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I agree with the minister on that point. Perhaps the minister will give a little better explanation on the committee as to why he is perpetuating this disunity as regards pension rights for the services.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Ask him if he will move the amendment himself.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Thank you very much.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

speechtext:
There are two or three things about this clause that I do not understand, and one is why there should be the difference in the time. I heard the remarks made about militia service, and I think any one who served in the militia during peace time knows it entailed a great deal of service given at night and on week-ends. In the years when we were coming nearer to war, the men who served in the milita spent a lot of time.
I was surprised when this amendment came in that there should be a change, of this kind. After the first great war it was considered that a, man who served in the militia should be given half-time for his permanent force pension. Today, on the ground of economy, I suppose, it is cut down to a quarter, and I do not think that is fair to those men who gave their time or to the men who are today giving their time in the militia.

That change was made last year.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I think the point made by the hon. member for Vancouver North deserves more consideration than so far the minister has seen fit to give it. One might point out that it would not impose a very great burden on the treasury, because these personnel are still required to make contributions at the time they make their election. So I think that technical point is not very important, as the minister may find out if he reconsiders it; and I see no good reason why it should not be adopted.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: I can assure the committee and the hon. member who has spoken that everything will be considered and reconsidered, that this process is going on continually. But with regard to this matter I am informed that it was thoroughly considered by an inter-departmental committee last year. It was considered by the government and was put forward to the house after all that consideration, and we are not prepared to make any further change at the present time. It is considered to be a fair proposal and, as I say, it should be read together with all of part V, which constitutes a whole that has been worked out to give a fair pension provision for the members of our active forces.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Could the minister give us the names of the personnel of this interdepartmental committee who set themselves up as authorities as to whether or not this act is streamlined for 1947? speechtext: Like other hon. members, I served in the non-permanent active militia on two separate occasions, once before serving in the first war and once after, and I appreciate very well the extent and value of their services. subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: That is not at all an answer to my question. subtopic: EXTENSION OF PROVISION OF ACT TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: It was felt that if you were to get any benefit in respect of pension from your service in the permanent force for the period spent in the non-permanent force, it should be in respect of service which was of direct value to your service in the permanent force. I
should like to point out to the minister that before the war there were in the auxiliary air force, for example, men serving as transport drivers andi getting exactly the same training they -would have been given in the army, serving as transport drivers. As a veteran I think

Standing Committees
I can congratulate the minister on his recent efforts to consolidate the transport services of the army, navy and air force, for example, the medical services, and so on. Here is something exactly along the same line. Before the war, there were only four auxiliary air force squadrons in Canada, and lads who did not live in the cities where those squadrons were located hadi no hope of giving service to their king and country ini the auxiliary air force. If they wanted to give service they had to join the militia or the naval reserve. When the war came on, they joined the air force. Now they are continuing in the permanent force, and the minister is trying to point out that their service was of very little value to the air force. I would think one of the best indications we could have that we are moving ahead to one consolidated armed service, under one minister, would be to recognize the young lad who, before 1939, wanted to serve in the non-permanent forces, whether army, navy or air force. The actual number of people involved must be very small. I should like to wager that only the air force is involved, because certainly no man who was in an air squadron before the war joined the army or navy. I know most men who were in the naval reserve joined the navy, but there were a number, a considerable number, who, as I have said, could not get into the air squadron and who joined the militia as the next best thing but who joined the air force when the war came. I suggest that it would be another step in this consolidation! of the three branches of our services into one united service to acknowledge this service in any branch.
